newsitem.title: RUSSIA: NATO, Russia clinch deal but doubt surrounds detail.
newsitem.headline: NATO, Russia clinch deal but doubt surrounds detail.

text.p: NATO and Russia agreed a deal on forging a peaceful new relationship between the former Cold War enemies on Wednesday, but behind the smiles of the negotiators doubts remained about the precise nature of the deal.
"Today in Moscow we have taken an historic step closer to a peaceful, undivided, democratic Europe for the first time in history," U.S. President Bill Clinton said in Washington.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov declared: "It is a big victory for reason, it is a big victory for the world community and it is a big victory for Russia and all governments in the world interested in peace and cooperation."

He clasped an arm around NATO Secretary General Javier Solana at a joint news conference in the garden of a foreign ministry mansion in Moscow after the breakthrough which ended months of negotiations described by Solana as "very tough".

President Boris Yeltsin, who has steered a precarious course between his allies in the West and Russian opinion indignant at NATO's plan to expand into eastern Europe, said he had won the support of Western leaders in a round of telephone diplomacy this week. He now hoped to sign a deal in Paris on May 27.
The document, known as the NATO-Russia Founding Act, must be approved by the 16 NATO member governments first.

It is not clear when details of the pact may become known. A joint statement said only that NATO and Russia had made "decisive progress" on key issues including military problems, which had been the main obstacles to agreement.
For the moment, both sides appeared content to welcome the fact of a deal after months of tense hard bargaining.
"Reason has prevailed. The road to signing on May 27 is clearly open," Solana said.
Yeltsin, apparently bracing for attacks from nationalist opponents, said the document would minimise the threat posed to Russia of former Soviet-bloc states being admitted to NATO.

"We are against expansion," the president said in a rare interview. "But considering the realities, both historic and, unfortunately, in real life, it has gone too far and we have to deal with this and minimise the risk for Russia."

Clearly addressing a domestic audience, Yeltsin indicated he had won the guarantees he sought to bind NATO to not moving its forces closer to Russia's borders and on giving the Kremlin a virtual veto on NATO decision-making.
"The binding nature of this document is clear to see," Yeltsin said, saying the Act would be similar to the 1975 Helsinki Act signed by the Soviet Union.
"Decisions can be taken only by consensus," Yeltsin said following the signing. "If Russia is against some decision, it means this decision will not go through."
Clinton, however, stressed: "Russia will work closely with NATO but not in NATO, giving Russia a voice but not a veto."

The 66-year-old Kremlin leader, looking relaxed as he sat outdoors in bright sunshine, also indicated NATO may have given pledges not to deploy forces in the territories of those former Soviet-bloc states likely to be given membership shortly.
"If military forces are not to be deployed in the new member states, then this is to be precisely observed," he said.
It was not clear, however, if he was referring to Russian demands or the actual treaty contents.
"Nuclear weapons are not to be deployed, no storage facilities are to be used, infrastructure abandoned by the Warsaw Pact is not to be used," Yeltsin added.
Primakov said the text of the agreement should be on President Boris Yeltsin's desk by the end of Wednesday. Solana was to forward the accord to NATO governments for approval.
NATO officials are anxious to conclude a deal with Russia before a Madrid summit in July at which the defence pact may invite Poland, Hungary, the Czech Republic or others to join.
Polish Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati said: "Poland welcomes the agreement...which is a basis for cooperation and lowering tensions in Europe."
But among Yeltsin's communist opponents who dominate the Russian parliament, reaction was cooler.
"(The West) has often cheated Russia and they will probably cheat us this time as well because we have nothing to trade with," Albert Makashov, a communist told reporters.
